doc.title: Chris Parker interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, January 5, 2023

title: Practicing by recording and Rudy Van Gelder's foam trick
summary: Parker records himself in his studio, recalls demo work in 1970s New York, and tells how Van Gelder taped foam to his leg to stop rim shots on an Esther Phillips CTI date.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Making records: studios, takes and the technology

blocks.x: Do you remember an early time, it might have been Lionel Hampton but doing a recording, doing a take then going behind the glass into the control room and listening back to yourself? Do you remember what that felt like?
Yeah. I suck. I suck. I’ve got to practice more.

Recording yourself, you know at my studio I have a rudimentary set up I mean a mic on the bass drum and an overhead mic. So it’s kind of like the way they recorded in the 30s or the 40s, you know one mic or maybe two mics. And record that, playing at different volumes and different feels and listen back and adjust accordingly. When I first got to New York in the 70s there was a lot, there was so much work around and a lot of it was demos, you know making demos for people. And it wasn’t in the A studios, it was in the, not home studios yet but much smaller studios. So those were always great opportunities to refine your recorded performances you know listening back and saying oh yeah, that snare drum might not be the right one or maybe I can take the padding off that snare drum, open it up a little bit more and it will translate better. I remember recording at Rudy Van Gelder’s, a CTI recording with Esther Phillips and Rudy Van Gelder was the engineer and you know on all those Blue Note records, I mean he was like a giant among engineers for all those Lee Morgan and Art Blakey and Grant Green I mean all those guys, Wes Montgomery records. So he came out after maybe one or two takes with this big piece of foam, a giant like piece of foam this thick and gaffer-taped it to my left leg. And I said, “What’s going on?” And he said, “Oh don’t worry about it, don’t worry about it.” So the next take we did I realized what he was doing. I was playing a rim shot, not intentionally but letting the stick hit the rim as well as the center of the drum every time I played two and four. So he put this piece of foam so that the butt of the stick could not go any further than — you know it was like three inches of foam. And I said aha. So he was getting a clear center of the drum sound as opposed to a rim shot. It made all the difference. You know when I listened back the next time I said wow, I’ve got to put that in my memory bank. © Fillius Jazz Archive -9-
You never forgot that, wow. And it’s interesting that he didn’t come out and tell you what you were doing, he just decided I’m going to fix this, I’m not going to screw around.
Exactly. And he did it with white gloves on. You know he was very —
And don’t touch my microphones, right?
Don’t touch my microphones, don’t touch my board.
